title: Chapter 30
paragraphs: Meanwhile Vassily Lukitch hadn't at first realized who the lady was, and gathered from their conversation that she was none other than the mother who had left her husband — whom he had never seen, since he had taken the post after her departure. He hesitated about whether to go in, or to send word to Alexey Alexandrovitch. Reflecting in the end that his duty was to get Seryozha up at the appointed hour, and that it was not his business to consider who was in the room — mother or anyone else — but simply to do his job, he finished dressing, went to the door, and opened it.
But the mother's and child's embraces, the sound of their voices, and what they were saying, made him change his mind.
He shook his head, sighed, and closed the door again. "I'll give it another ten minutes," he said to himself, clearing his throat and wiping his eyes.

Among the household servants there was intense excitement all this while. Everyone had heard that their mistress was back, that Kapitonitch had let her in, and that she was at that very moment in the nursery. They all knew the master always went in person to the nursery at nine, and they all understood perfectly that the husband and wife could not be allowed to meet, and that they must prevent it. Korney, the valet, went down to the porter's room, asked who had let her in and how it had happened, and on learning that Kapitonitch had admitted her and shown her up, gave the old man a piece of his mind. The hall-porter was stubbornly silent, but when Korney told him he ought to be sacked, Kapitonitch shot up to him, waved his hands in Korney's face, and started:

"Oh yes, of course you wouldn't have let her in! After ten years' service, never a hard word from her, and now you'd come out with, 'Off with you, get out, get going!' Oh yes, you're a sharp one at politics, no doubt! You don't need to be taught how to swindle the master and lift fur coats!"

"Soldier!" Korney said with contempt, and turned to the nurse, who was just coming in. "Here, what do you make of this, Marya Efimovna — he let her in without a word to anyone," Korney said to her. "Alexey Alexandrovitch will be down any minute now — and he'll go straight into the nursery!"
"A fine business, a fine business!" said the nurse. "You'd best find some way to delay him, Korney Vassilievitch — keep the master back — while I go and get her out somehow. A fine business!"

When the nurse came into the nursery, Seryozha was telling his mother how he and Nadinka had taken a tumble going downhill in the sledge and had turned over three times. She was listening to the sound of his voice, watching his face and the play of expression on it, holding his hand, but she wasn't following what he was saying. She had to go, she had to leave him — that was the only thing she was thinking and feeling. She heard Vassily Lukitch's footsteps come up to the door, then his cough; she heard the nurse's footsteps approaching too. But she sat as if turned to stone, unable to begin speaking or to get up.
"Mistress, darling!" the nurse began, going up to Anna and kissing her hands and shoulders. "God's brought joy to our boy on his birthday after all. You haven't changed one bit."
"Oh, dear nurse, I didn't know you were in the house," said Anna, rousing herself for a moment.
"I'm not living here, I'm living with my daughter. I came for the birthday, Anna Arkadyevna, darling!"
The nurse suddenly burst into tears and started kissing her hand again.

Seryozha, his eyes shining and a smile on his face, was holding his mother by one hand and his nurse by the other, pattering on the rug with his fat little bare feet. The tenderness his beloved nurse was showing his mother had thrown him into an ecstasy.

"Mother! She often comes to see me, and when she does…" he was starting to say — then stopped, noticing that the nurse was whispering something to his mother, and that on his mother's face there was a look of fear and something like shame, which sat so strangely on her.
She went up to him.
"My sweet!" she said.

She couldn't bring herself to say _good-bye_, but the look on her face said it, and he understood. "Darling, darling Kootik!" — she used the name she had called him by when he was little — "you won't forget me? You.…" but she couldn't go on.

How often afterward she thought of the things she could have said. But now she didn't know how to say it, and could say nothing. Yet Seryozha understood everything she wanted to tell him. He understood that she was unhappy and that she loved him. He even understood what the nurse had whispered. He had caught the words "always at nine o'clock," and he knew that this was about his father, and that his father and mother couldn't meet. He understood all that — only one thing he couldn't understand: why was there a look of fear and shame on her face? She wasn't in the wrong, and yet she was afraid of him and ashamed of something. He would have liked to ask a question that would clear up that doubt, but he didn't dare; he could see that she was miserable, and he felt for her. Silently he pressed himself against her and whispered, "Don't go yet. He won't come yet."

The mother held him away from her to see what he was thinking, and what to say to him. In his frightened face she read not only that he was talking about his father, but that he was, in a sense, asking her what he ought to think about his father.
"Seryozha, my darling," she said, "love him. He's better and kinder than I am, and I've done him wrong. When you're grown up you'll judge it."

"There's no one better than you!" he cried in despair through his tears, and, gripping her by the shoulders, he started squeezing her against him with all his strength, his arms shaking with the effort.
"My sweet, my little one!" said Anna, and she cried as helplessly and childishly as he was crying.
At that moment the door opened. Vassily Lukitch came in.
From the other door came the sound of footsteps, and the nurse said in a frightened whisper, "He's coming," and handed Anna her hat.

Seryozha sank down on the bed and sobbed, hiding his face in his hands. Anna pulled his hands away, kissed his wet face one more time, and walked quickly to the door. Alexey Alexandrovitch came in, meeting her. Seeing her, he stopped short and bowed his head.

Even though she had just said he was better and kinder than she was, in the quick glance she shot at him, taking in every detail of his figure, feelings of revulsion and hatred toward him, and jealousy over her son, took hold of her. With a swift movement she dropped her veil and, picking up her pace, almost ran out of the room.
She didn't have time to undo it, and so carried back with her the parcel of toys she had picked out the day before, with such love and sorrow, in the toy shop.
